subtopic: Methods of Evaluation of Definite Integrals
stem: If \(\int_{0}^{k}\frac{1}{2 + 8x^{2}}dx = \ \frac{\pi}{16}\), then the value of \(k\) is ______.
solution:
**(A)** \(k=\dfrac{1}{2}\)

Take the coefficient of \(x^{2}\) out of the denominator: \(2+8x^{2}=8\left(x^{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)=8\left[x^{2}+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]\).

\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{k}\dfrac{dx}{2+8x^{2}}=\dfrac{1}{8}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{k}\dfrac{dx}{x^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}=\dfrac{1}{8}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{\frac{1}{2}}\right]_{0}^{k}=\dfrac{1}{4}\left[\tan^{-1}2x\right]_{0}^{k}\)

\(=\dfrac{1}{4}\left[\tan^{-1}2k-\tan^{-1}0\right]=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}2k\)

Equating to the given value: \(\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}2k=\dfrac{\pi}{16}\), so \(\tan^{-1}2k=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), giving \(2k=\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}=1\).

\(\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{2}\), which is option (A).

Check: with \(k=\frac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}(1)=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{16}\), the stated value.

**(D)** \(0\)

The limits are symmetric about the origin, so test the integrand for parity. Let \(f(x)=x^{3}\sin^{4}x\).

\(f(-x)=(-x)^{3}\sin^{4}(-x)=-x^{3}\left(-\sin x\right)^{4}=-x^{3}\sin^{4}x=-f(x)\)

(here \(\sin^{4}(-x)=\left(-\sin x\right)^{4}=\sin^{4}x\), an even factor, multiplied by the odd factor \(x^{3}\)).

So \(f\) is an odd function, and by the property \(\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=0\) when \(f\) is odd,

\(k=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}x^{3}\sin^{4}x\,dx=0\), which is option (D).

The integrand carries \(\sqrt{x}\) both inside the sine and in the denominator, and \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\) is, up to a constant, the derivative of \(\sqrt{x}\). That is the signal for the substitution

\(t = \sqrt{x}\)

Then

\(dt = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,dx\)  so  \(\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = 2\,dt\)

Substituting,

\(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\sin\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx = \int\sin t \cdot 2\,dt = 2\int\sin t\,dt = -2\cos t + c\)

Restoring \(t = \sqrt{x}\):

\(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\sin\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx = -2\cos\sqrt{x} + c\)

**Verification by differentiating the answer back:**

\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-2\cos\sqrt{x}\right) = -2\left(-\sin\sqrt{x}\right) \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{x}\right) = 2\sin\sqrt{x} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{\sin\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}}\)

The integrand is recovered exactly.

Use \(\cos 2x=2\cos^{2}x-1\), i.e. \(\cos^{2}x=\dfrac{1+\cos 2x}{2}\).

\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2}x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left(1+\cos 2x\right)dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x+\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\)

\(=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\dfrac{\sin\pi}{2}\right)-\left(0+\dfrac{\sin 0}{2}\right)\right]=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}+0-0\right]\)

\(\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2}x\,dx=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)

Check: over \(\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\cos^{2}x\) and \(\sin^{2}x\) enclose equal areas and their sum is \(1\), so each must equal \(\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) - the same value.

Rationalise the integrand by multiplying numerator and denominator by \(1+\sin x\):

\(\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\left(1-\sin x\right)\left(1+\sin x\right)}=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{1-\sin^{2}x}=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^{2}x}=\sec^{2}x+\sec x\tan x\)

\(\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\dfrac{dx}{1-\sin x}=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\sec^{2}x+\sec x\tan x\right)dx=\left[\tan x+\sec x\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\)

At \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\sec\dfrac{\pi}{4}=1+\sqrt{2}\).
At \(x=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+\sec\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=-1+\sqrt{2}\).

\(=\left(1+\sqrt{2}\right)-\left(-1+\sqrt{2}\right)=2\)

\(\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\,dx=2\)

Check on the antiderivative: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tan x+\sec x\right)=\sec^{2}x+\sec x\tan x=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^{2}x}=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\), the integrand. The integrand is continuous on \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right]\) (it is never \(1-\sin x=0\) there), so the Fundamental Theorem applies.

Split the interval \([0,2a]\) at \(a\), using \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{c}=\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}+\displaystyle\int_{b}^{c}\):

\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx+\displaystyle\int_{a}^{2a}f(x)\,dx\)   ... (I)

In the second integral put \(x=2a-t\), so \(dx=-dt\).

Changing the limits: when \(x=a\), \(t=a\); when \(x=2a\), \(t=0\).

\(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{a}^{0}f(2a-t)\left(-dt\right)=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(2a-t)\,dt\)

Since a definite integral does not depend on the name of the variable of integration, \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(2a-t)\,dt=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(2a-x)\,dx\).

Substituting in (I):

\(\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(2a-x)\,dx\)

which is the required result.

Check with \(f(x)=x\), \(a=1\): the left side is \(\int_{0}^{2}x\,dx=2\); the right side is \(\int_{0}^{1}x\,dx+\int_{0}^{1}(2-x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2}=2\). The two agree.

The identity as printed cannot be proved, because with the upper limit \(\pi\) the integral does not exist — see the errata note. What IS provable, and what the stated right-hand side is exactly the value of, is the classical result with upper limit \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). That is proved first, and the failure of the printed limit is then set out.

**To show:  \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left(1 + \tan x\right)dx = \dfrac{\pi}{8}\log 2\).**

Let

\(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left(1 + \tan x\right)dx\)   ...(i)

Apply the property \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(a - x)\,dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\):

\(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left(1 + \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right)\right)dx\)   ...(ii)

Now simplify the integrand of (ii). Since

\(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right) = \dfrac{\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \tan x}{1 + \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\tan x} = \dfrac{1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x}\)

we get

\(1 + \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right) = 1 + \dfrac{1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x} = \dfrac{\left(1 + \tan x\right) + \left(1 - \tan x\right)}{1 + \tan x} = \dfrac{2}{1 + \tan x}\)

Substituting into (ii) and splitting the logarithm,

\(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left(\dfrac{2}{1 + \tan x}\right)dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log 2\,dx - \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\left(1 + \tan x\right)dx\)

The second integral is \(I\) itself by (i), and the first is \(\log 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Hence

\(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\log 2 - I\)

\(2I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\log 2\)

\(I = \dfrac{\pi}{8}\log 2\)

as required. Every step is legitimate here: on \(\left[0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\), \(\tan x\) increases from 0 to 1, so \(1 + \tan x\) stays between 1 and 2 and the logarithm is defined, continuous and bounded throughout.

**Why the printed upper limit cannot work.** Over \([0,\ \pi]\) the integrand breaks down three separate ways:

1. \(\tan x\) is undefined at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), where it has an infinite discontinuity.
2. For \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\), \(\tan x < -1\), so \(1 + \tan x < 0\) and \(\log\left(1 + \tan x\right)\) is undefined over the real numbers.
3. At \(x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\), \(\tan x = -1\), so \(1 + \tan x = 0\) and \(\log\left(1 + \tan x\right) \to -\infty\).

So no real value at all can be assigned to \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\log\left(1 + \tan x\right)dx\), and the printed identity is not merely false but meaningless as written.

stem: Prove that: \(\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx + \int_{0}^{a}f(2a - x)dx\). Hence show that: \(\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin xdx = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin xdx\).
solution:
**Proof.** Split the interval \([0,2a]\) at \(a\):

\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx+\displaystyle\int_{a}^{2a}f(x)\,dx\)   ... (I)

In the second integral put \(x=2a-t\), so \(dx=-dt\); when \(x=a\), \(t=a\), and when \(x=2a\), \(t=0\).

\(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{a}^{0}f(2a-t)\left(-dt\right)=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(2a-t)\,dt=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(2a-x)\,dx\)

(the variable of integration in a definite integral is a dummy). Substituting in (I):

\(\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(2a-x)\,dx\)

**Hence the deduction.** Take \(f(x)=\sin x\) and \(2a=\pi\), so \(a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\):

\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin\left(\pi-x\right)dx\)

Since \(\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x\), the second integral equals the first:

\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx\)

\(\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx\)

Check by direct evaluation: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi}=1+1=2\), and \(2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx=2\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}=2(0+1)=2\). The two sides agree.

stem: Prove that: \(\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx = \int_{a}^{b}f(a + b - x)dx\). Hence evaluate: \(\int_{0}^{3}\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{3 - x}}dx\).
solution:
**Proof.** In \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)\,dx\) put \(t=a+b-x\), so \(dt=-dx\).

Changing the limits: when \(x=a\), \(t=b\); when \(x=b\), \(t=a\).

\(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{b}^{a}f(t)\left(-dt\right)=\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(t)\,dt\)

Since the variable of integration is a dummy, \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(t)\,dt=\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\).

\(\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-x)\,dx\)

**Hence the evaluation.** Let \(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3-x}}\,dx\).

Here \(a=0\), \(b=3\), so \(a+b-x=3-x\). Applying the property just proved:

\(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}\dfrac{\sqrt{3-x}}{\sqrt{3-x}+\sqrt{3-(3-x)}}\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}\dfrac{\sqrt{3-x}}{\sqrt{3-x}+\sqrt{x}}\,dx\)   ... (II)

Adding the original integral and (II):

\(2I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}\dfrac{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3-x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3-x}}\,dx=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}1\,dx=\left[x\right]_{0}^{3}=3\)

\(\therefore\ I=\dfrac{3}{2}\)

Check: the integrand takes the value \(\frac{1}{2}\) at the midpoint \(x=\frac{3}{2}\) and the two halves of the interval contribute symmetrically, so the mean value of the integrand over \([0,3]\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\) and the integral is \(\frac{1}{2}\times 3=\frac{3}{2}\) - the same value.
